what: Motor A turns a shaft inside a 24-tooth friction clutch. Its outer teeth drive a 40-tooth output on motor B. The shaft pointers and clutch ring can move separately. A drives a 24-tooth slipping clutch and 40-tooth output; B returns the output to zero and holds it, then releases it.
try: Reset, load the program and Run. Watch the unloaded output turn opposite to the input.
B returns the output to zero and holds it. Watch A continue turning while the clutch ring and output settle to a stop.
B releases the output, then A reverses. Check that motion returns and the free output/input speed ratio is approximately −0.6.
why: The clutch transmits torque through limited friction rather than a rigid axle connection. Under a light load its ring follows the shaft. When the holding load exceeds the friction limit, the shaft slips inside the ring. The model uses a nominal 0.0375 N·m threshold; it does not predict the wear-dependent torque of an individual real part.
matters: Torque limiters can protect a mechanism when an output is blocked. Slip loses angular indexing, and real clutches dissipate work as heat; this example has no temperature model.
question: Must the input shaft stop whenever the output is held still?
answer: No. Above the clutch limit, the input shaft can keep turning relative to its stationary toothed ring. Releasing the load restores transmission, but does not undo the angle lost during slip.
further: Use the two manual motor controls to compare assistance and opposition at low speeds. Stop All holds both shafts.
Compare the slipping clutch with a rigid gear train: a tooth-count ratio applies between the outer ring and output, even when the input shaft slips.
formula: Free transmission: ωB / ωA ≈ −24 / 40 = −0.6; nominal slip torque = 0.0375 N·m
